"""
LRU Cache with TTL Expiry and Thread Safety

This module implements a Least Recently Used (LRU) cache with Time-To-Live (TTL)
expiry functionality. It provides a thread-safe wrapper around the cache implementation
and includes a comprehensive pytest test suite.

Key Features:
- LRU eviction policy: When the cache reaches its capacity, the least recently used
  item is evicted to make room for new items.
- TTL (Time-To-Live): Each cached item has an associated expiration time. Items that
  have exceeded their TTL are considered expired and will be evicted either lazily
  (on access) or eagerly (via periodic cleanup).
- Thread Safety: All public methods are thread-safe, allowing concurrent access from
  multiple threads without data corruption or race conditions.
- Lazy and Eager Expiration: Expired items are removed lazily when accessed. Additionally,
  an optional background thread can perform eager cleanup at configurable intervals.
- Configurable Parameters: Users can customize cache capacity, default TTL, expiration
  check interval, and thread safety settings.

Usage Example:
    from lru_cache_ttl import LRUCacheWithTTL

    # Create a cache with capacity 100 and default TTL of 60 seconds
    cache = LRUCacheWithTTL(max_size=100, ttl=60)

    # Set a value with custom TTL of 120 seconds
    cache.set('key1', 'value1', ttl=120)

    # Get a value (returns None if not found or expired)
    value = cache.get('key1')

    # Delete a value
    cache.delete('key1')

    # Clear all entries
    cache.clear()

    # Get cache statistics
    stats = cache.get_stats()
    print(stats)

The module also includes a pytest test suite that covers:
- Basic get/set/delete operations
- LRU eviction behavior
- TTL expiry (lazy and eager)
- Thread safety under concurrent access
- Edge cases (empty cache, single element, large capacity)
- Error handling and invalid inputs
- Statistics and metadata tracking
- Background cleanup thread management

To run the tests:
    pytest lru_cache_ttl.py -v

note: Splash 1.4.0, the release tarball (splash-1.4.0-arm64-macos26.tar.gz from github.com/incoai/splash/releases, unpacked; SPLASH_ROOT, by default where `brew install incoai/tap/splash` puts the same tree), served with `splash serve` (install/launcher.py, the command the Homebrew wrapper runs). Splash takes only Hugging Face repo ids for --model, so the harness links the model folder's files into a Hub-cache-shaped snapshot in {state} (nace-local/... is a local name, not a Hub repo; the revision is the SHA-1 of that name) and points HF_HUB_CACHE there; with --offline and a 40-hex --revision it asks the Hub for nothing. The MTP head and the drafter folder are not linked (Splash never reads MTP heads). Its DFlash2 drafter for this model, incoai/Qwen3.6-35B-A3B-DFlash2 (the one Kapitsa reads), is named as a local directory with --draft-model, so a missing drafter fails the run instead of starting a download. Otherwise Splash's own defaults: DFlash2 speculation, always on (one draft pass proposes a 7-token chain, verified exactly; on this mixture of experts a verify budget learned over earlier cycles picks the rows, --verify-rows auto, hence the three extra warm-up decodes), INT8 KV, FP32 recurrent state, the SSD prefix cache at its automatic quota (temporary files, gone at exit). --expert-memory off keeps every routed expert resident (1.4.0 can stream experts from the SSD; its automatic setting also loads them all where memory holds them, as here). --max-context 32K like the other engines; --language-only (text only, no vision preparation); --idle-release off (by default an idle server frees its weights after 10 minutes); --no-webui. Inherited SPLASH_* variables (API key, port, reasoning defaults) are cleared.
